newsitem.title: HONG KONG: OPINION - Bismuth demand to double, prices to rise.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Bismuth demand to double, prices to rise.

text.p: By Frank Fauche, managing director
Ferromin Limited
Consumption of bismuth has grown a phenomenal 50 percent since 1992, the fastest growth rate of any non-ferrous metal, and has the potential to double again in the next five years.
With research for new applications ranging from additives to lubricants, pharmaceuticals and electronics to consumer goods, the main constraint on the market is supply.
Bismuth is set to become a 10,000-tonne-a-year market within the next five years -- a 100 percent increase over present levels.

Most new applications are shelved in the early stages of research because producers fear for long-term supply. But more and more smaller applications are winning approval and this is steadily putting pressure on supply.

The only factor which can change this is the price level which needs to reach higher average levels to encourage new production and new production techniques. Most current applications could accept higher prices and a per-pound price of
US$4.00-5.00 is a very realistic level to aim for as the next trading range.
Indeed, not only are these price levels realistic, they are necessary for further development of the market and 1997 will be the year bismuth prices hit greater heights.
THE SHORT TERM OUTLOOK
The market is in a much tighter situation than most observers believe due to the following factors:
-- Mexico and Peru are sold out to June/July with no expectation of short-term availability.
-- Cominco is sold out up to October/November.
-- There are still shorts in the market who will need to cover borrowed material from delayed contracts.
-- The only place bismuth is still availabile is China, although stocks there are estimated to be either less than or around 100 tonnes, which is historically low.
-- There is little availablilty in the major consumers the United States, Japan and Europe.
-- There is no possibility for a rapid supply increase by any of the major producers.
-- Prices have increased recently in view of the above factors which are a pure consequence of supply and demand.

Further price evolution will now depend solely on the reaction of the consumer. To date, very few consumers have reacted to the new situation, although some have started to enquire for additional quantities with producers and trading companies.

We expect prices to either move up gradually to the new trading range as stock in all segments of the pipeline are low. If consumers decide to rebuild inventories -- and a few have already correctly done so -- prices will rise faster to the $4.0-5.0 per lb level.
THE LONG TERM OUTLOOK

Accelerated growth will continue and the market looks forward to an early decision from Corriente to start exploiting the Tasna mine in Bolivia. These quantities will be necessary in the next two to three years in order to feed growing demand.
The market is therefore looking for a new trading range within $4.00 to $5.00 per lb which will enable Corriente to make a decision to bring Tasna on line.

Another potentially large supplier which could increase capacity is China, through efficiencies in production and recovery of very low grades of bismuth in both the lead and gold industries. These grades, however, are so low that at current
prices there is absolutely no motivation to do this.

As it will take at least two to three years before Tasna will be operational from the day the decision to go ahead is made and the larger Chinese supply will only come on stream if higher prices warrant the investment, there might be extreme volatility in the market if new supplies do not come on stream in the next few years and it is not unreasonable to expect wild swings between $5.00 and $10.00 per lb.

It should be remembered that this assumption is based on the fact that China, Mexico and Peru will account for the bulk of world production now that Asarco is out of play. In the past, there have been production disruptions in these areas for a number of reasons including natural disasters.

Moreover, as bismuth production is concentrated in the hands of a few players, they will have to show better returns on their operations and bismuth will not be merely a by-product that can be sold at any price.

As the new applications mature over the next few years and other applications come on stream, bismuth will be entering a new era of higher prices which should motivate enhancement of production, which will be necessary for growing demand.
(NOTE - The views expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the view of Reuters).
